tour.title: Kathmandu: Gods, Kings and Living Goddesses
tour.summary: A living goddess, Malla kings, hippie lanes and market squares — ending with the 365-step climb to the all-seeing eyes of Swayambhunath.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to Kathmandu, a city where the gods are not metaphors. They live here. One of them is a small girl who lives in a palace on this square, and you are about to stand in her courtyard.

A word on the country around the temples, because it explains the scaffolding you will see. Nepal was a Hindu kingdom until very recently — a decade-long Maoist war ended in 2006, the 240-year-old monarchy was voted out in 2008, and the republic that followed was still finding its feet when the 2015 earthquake killed nine thousand people and flattened much of what you are about to walk through. What was rebuilt, what is still braced with timber, and what was lost — that is all part of the tour. Through all of it, Hindus and Buddhists here have mostly shared gods, festivals and streets without asking anyone to choose. That easy overlap is the real religion of Kathmandu.

Here is the shape of the walk. We start in Kathmandu Durbar Square, the old royal plaza of the Malla kings, where every building is competing for your attention and most of them are winning. You will meet the living goddess Kumari, the palace of the monkey god's gate, the wooden pavilion that gave this entire city its name, and two triple-roofed temples that survived everything including the 2015 earthquake. Then we drift south into Freak Street, where the hippies of 1970 came looking for enlightenment and mostly found hashish, before turning west through the market squares of Indra Chowk and Jana Bahal, where the shopping has not fundamentally changed in four hundred years.

And then the finale, which is also a workout. The hill of Swayambhunath rises ahead of you, and the only correct way up is the old eastern stairway: 365 steps, one for every day of the year, with the monkeys judging your fitness all the way. At the top waits one of the oldest stupas on earth, painted with the calmest, most famous eyes in Asia.

It is about four kilometres, plus the climb. Three to four hours at a stroll, longer if you go inside the palace museum, which you should. Two house rules. Rule one: ticket prices move. I will quote rupees, but anything I say about money is an educated guess — verify at the gate and never blame the nice voice in your ear. Rule two: this is a living religious city, not a theme park. Take your shoes off where asked, walk clockwise around every stupa and shrine, and do not point your feet at anyone's gods.
tour.difficulty: Easy and flat through Durbar Square and the market lanes, then a real climb: 365 steep stone steps up Swayambhu hill with no shade. Take it slowly and carry water.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 8:30 to 9am, so you reach Swayambhu before the midday haze and heat. Mornings are also when the Kumari sometimes appears at her window, and the light on the stupa's eyes is at its best.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Kumari Ghar, House of the Living Goddess
stops.narration:
Look at that carved wooden window on the upper floor. Behind it, quite possibly watching you right now, is a goddess. A real one. A small girl, somewhere between four and ten years old, who is worshipped as the living incarnation of the warrior goddess Taleju, and you are standing in her front yard.

Here is how it works. The Kumari is chosen from young girls of the Shakya caste through a series of trials that are genuinely nerve-racking — tradition says the candidates must spend a night among sacrificed animals without showing fear, and show the thirty-two perfections of a goddess, right down to eyelashes like a cow's. The winner moves into this palace, leaves it only a handful of times a year for festivals, and is carried everywhere, because her feet must never touch the ground outside. When she reaches puberty, she retires with a pension and a mortal life, and the search begins again.

The building itself is a jewel: a three-storey brick and timber palace from the 1700s with some of the finest woodcarving in the valley, arranged around the courtyard you are standing in. During the Indra Jatra festival in September, the Kumari appears at that window in full regalia while the whole city cheers, and the king of Nepal — back when there was one — came here to receive her blessing, which tells you exactly where the power sits.

Two rules, and both matter. First: she sometimes appears at the window in the morning, and if she does, you may look, you may even receive a blessing glance, but you may not photograph her. No photo of the Kumari herself, ever. Photograph the courtyard, the carvings, the window — everything except the goddess. Second: keep your voice down in here. A goddess is trying to have a childhood.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The courtyard is free to enter during the day. Entry is covered by the general Durbar Square area; no separate Kumari ticket. Verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Courtyard generally open in daylight hours. The Kumari appears at the window unpredictably, most reliably in the morning and during festivals such as Indra Jatra.
stops.accessibility: Step-free into the courtyard from the lane, but the surface is old brick and uneven. The upper floors are not open to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Come back during Indra Jatra in September if you can: the Kumari is paraded in a chariot right past this door, and the whole square turns into the biggest party of the Nepali year.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard and walk north across the square, past the statue on the tall pillar, towards the palace wing with the Hanuman statue beside its gate. That is Hanuman Dhoka, about a minute away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sundar1, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hanuman Dhoka Palace
stops.narration:
See the orange statue smeared with vermilion paste beside the gate? That is Hanuman, the monkey god, standing guard since 1672, and this whole palace is named after him: Hanuman Dhoka, the Hanuman Gate. You do not get named after your bouncer unless the bouncer is excellent.

This was the royal palace of Kathmandu for centuries — first the Malla kings, then the Shah dynasty that unified Nepal. Kings were crowned in its Nasal Chowk courtyard right up into modern times, and the palace grew the way power grows: one courtyard, then another, then a tower, then a taller tower because the king next door built one. The nine-storey Basantapur Tower from the 1700s was the valley's skyscraper, and on a clear day its upper windows frame the Himalayas like somebody hung them there.

Go inside if you can. The palace is now a museum, and its courtyards are the good stuff: carved wooden struts where every beam end is a different god or demon pulling a face, the coronation courtyard, royal beds you are not allowed to nap on, and photographs of a court that wore jewelled top hats and carried swords to brunch. Parts of the complex were badly hurt in the 2015 earthquake and the scaffolding only recently came down, which is worth remembering when you look at the fresh timber — you are seeing a palace being reborn in real time.

And spare a thought for the Hanuman statue as you leave. For three and a half centuries, devotees have smeared him with orange paste for luck. He is less a statue now than a sculpture of devotion itself, several centimetres thick.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay around Rs 1,000 for the Durbar Square ticket, which covers the palace museum courtyards. SAARC nationals pay less. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Palace museum roughly 09:00 to 17:00 daily. The outer square is open access at all hours.
stops.accessibility: The museum courtyards involve steps, narrow doorways and uneven old stone. The nine-storey tower climb is steep ladders and not for everyone.
stops.insiderTip: The Tribhuvan Museum section inside holds the king's thrones and crown jewels crowds walk straight past — slow down there, it is the quietest room in the palace.
stops.nextStopDirections: Exit the palace gate and walk south-west across the square, past the tall Maju Dega temple on your right, towards the long low restored pavilion at the square's south-west corner. That is Kasthamandap, about two minutes away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Safalphotos, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kasthamandap Pavilion
stops.narration:
You are looking at the building this entire city is named after. Kathmandu is just Kasthamandap with seven centuries of mumbling applied. Say it slowly: Kas-tha-man-dap. Kath-mandu. The city is the souvenir.

The legend is magnificent. They say this three-storeyed pavilion was built from the timber of a single tree — one tree, one building — back in the 1100s or 1200s, and that a wandering sage dreamed the whole design. For centuries it served as the valley's great public living room: travellers slept here, merchants closed deals under its roof, festivals gathered at its steps. If old Kathmandu had a town square with a roof on it, this was the roof.

Then, in April 2015, the earthquake took it down completely. The collapse was one of the defining images of the disaster. And here is the part that gets me: the city rebuilt it the hard way — traditional methods, traditional materials, master woodcarvers recutting every strut, and the grand reopening finally came in 2022. What you are looking at is barely a few years old and eight hundred years old at the same time.

Walk around it slowly and look at the wood. The carved struts under the eaves are a whole mythology in timber — gods, wrestlers, demons, erotic couples, all holding up the roof with tremendous enthusiasm. Then look at the plinth. People still leave offerings here daily, because a building does not need to be ancient to be sacred. It just needs to be loved, and this one very clearly is.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the Durbar Square foreign-visitor ticket (around Rs 1,000; verify at the gate). No separate fee to walk around and under the pavilion.
stops.openingHours: Open access in daylight hours as part of the square.
stops.accessibility: Level ground around the pavilion with some uneven old paving. The raised plinth has steps and no ramp.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the Gorakhnath shrine inside the pavilion's ground floor — the ascetic god's image is why sadhus still gather here, and it is easy to miss behind the columns.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north-east back towards the centre of the square, about fifty metres, to the tall triple-roofed Vishnu temple with the gilded doorway. That is Trailokya Mohan.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Chainwit., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Trailokya Mohan Narayan Temple
stops.narration:
This slender triple-roofed pagoda is dedicated to Narayan — Vishnu, the preserver — under his name as Trailokya Mohan, the enchanter of the three worlds. Which is a strong name for a building, and the building earns it.

It was raised in the 1600s, in the great age of the Malla kings, when Kathmandu's rulers competed in temple-building the way modern cities compete in stadiums. King Pratap Malla's era turned this square into an architectural arms race, and this temple was one of its trophies: three diminishing roofs stacked like a wedding cake, brick walls, and a gilded doorway that glows even on a cloudy day. The pagoda style you see here — tiered roofs, broad eaves, carved struts — is Nepal's great gift to Asian architecture, and this is one of its purest examples.

Like everything on this square, it fell hard in 2015 and has been painstakingly rebuilt, so the crisp timber and fresh gilding you see are the restoration doing its job. Non-Hindus generally admire from the plinth rather than entering the sanctum, and honestly the exterior is the show: walk all the way around and read the struts. Each wooden bracket is a carved figure — deities, dancers, guardians — and the Malla carvers loved hiding jokes and grimaces in the corners.

One more thing to notice: the temple's position. It stands at the hinge between the palace quarter and the market quarter, gods facing commerce across fifty metres of paving. That is Kathmandu's whole philosophy in one sightline. The sacred and the everyday were never separated here. They just share the square.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the Durbar Square foreign-visitor ticket (around Rs 1,000; verify at the gate). The sanctum is for Hindu worshippers; visitors admire from outside.
stops.openingHours: Exterior visible at all hours; the square is open access. The shrine opens for worship in the morning and evening.
stops.accessibility: Viewed from the level square. The temple plinth itself is stepped with no ramp.
stops.insiderTip: Stand back at the Kasthamandap side at dusk: the gilded doorway catches the last light and the whole temple glows against the darkening brick.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk a few steps north to the biggest triple-roofed temple on the square, rising from a tall nine-stepped platform. That is Maju Dega, right beside you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sumobie, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Maju Dega Temple
stops.narration:
Now climb. Not all the way — just find a few steps of that tall nine-tiered platform and sit down, because this is the square's great grandstand and you have earned the view.

Maju Dega is the biggest temple on the square, a triple-roofed Shiva shrine raised in 1692 by Riddhi Lakshmi, the queen mother of the era, which tells you something about who really ran things. Nine stepped terraces lift it above the crowd, and from the top steps the whole plaza spreads out below you: the palace to the north, the Kumari's palace to the south, pigeons doing whatever pigeons do in the middle. Generations of Kathmandu teenagers have met on these steps, and you can see why. It is the best seat in the city.

The temple has had a dramatic few years. The 2015 earthquake damaged it badly, the roofs came off, the gods went into storage, and the restoration took years of carving and gilding to put right. What you see now is the result: fresh timber, gleaming roofs, and struts recarved by masters who learned from masters who learned from the men who carved the originals.

Here is my favourite detail. The platform's steps double as the square's noticeboard, meeting point and lunch spot all at once. Monument conservationists elsewhere would faint. Here it is simply understood that a temple works hardest when people use it. So sit for a minute. Watch the square work. Then we are leaving royalty behind and heading for the hippies — Freak Street is two minutes south, and the seventies are waiting.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the Durbar Square foreign-visitor ticket (around Rs 1,000; verify at the gate). Sitting on the lower steps is free and expected.
stops.openingHours: Exterior and steps accessible at all hours within the square.
stops.accessibility: The platform is nine steep stepped tiers with no handrail or ramp. The square around it is level but cobbled and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Climb only as high as feels safe — the upper tiers are steep with big drops and no rails. The third or fourth level already gives the full panorama.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south out of the square, past the Kumari Ghar corner, and follow the lane downhill for about two minutes into the narrow street of old guesthouses and guitar shops. That is Freak Street, old Jhochhen.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jan Kranendonk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Freak Street (Jhochhen)
stops.narration:
Smell that? Incense, butter tea, exhaust fumes, and the faint ghost of patchouli. Welcome to Freak Street — officially Jhochhen, but nobody under seventy calls it that — the most famous dead-end of the hippie trail.

In the late sixties and early seventies, this narrow lane was the end of the world. Kids from London and California rode buses and thumb across entire continents to get here, and what they found was astonishing: legal hashish shops with menus, cheap guesthouses with names like the Eden, and a city that mostly shrugged and let them get on with it. The shops sold state-licensed hashish the way Amsterdam would decades later — Kathmandu invented the concept and then, under international pressure, banned it all in 1973, ending the party in a single decree.

The freaks left, but the street kept the name and the attitude. Today's Jhochhen is guesthouses and trekking-gear shops, thangka painters and guitar makers, rooftop restaurants and bakeries doing heroic things with yak cheese. It is scruffier and kinder than Thamel, the tourist quarter that stole its crown, and the shopkeepers have stories if you have time.

Do one thing here: stop for tea. Any of the rooftop places will do. Order a milk chiya, look south over the jumble of brick and tin towards the hills, and consider that you are sitting where the sixties ended. Then finish your tea, because we are heading west into the markets, and Indra Chowk does not slow down for nostalgia.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A public lane. Your only expense will be tea and whatever the guitar shops talk you into.
stops.openingHours: Always open as a street. Shops roughly 09:00 to 20:00; rooftops serve until late evening.
stops.accessibility: A narrow lane with uneven paving and occasional motorbikes threading through. Step-free along its length but crowded.
stops.insiderTip: The thangka painting shops here will unroll anything if you ask — even if you are not buying, watching a master explain the iconography is a free masterclass.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head back north to the square's south edge, then walk north-west through the bazaar lanes for about five minutes, following signs for Indra Chowk. The big open market square with the temple on its platform is your next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Holynow, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Indra Chowk and Akash Bhairav
stops.narration:
Take a breath, because the quiet part of the walk is over. This is Indra Chowk, Kathmandu's great downtown crossroads, and it has been loud like this for centuries.

The square is a permanent festival of commerce: beads and bangles, marigold garlands, copper pots, saris, spices by the sack, and shopkeepers who have occupied the same three square metres since their grandfathers did. During festival season the whole place drowns in marigolds and the lanes smell like a flower shop exploded. This is also where the Kumari's chariot processes during Indra Jatra, so the living goddess you met an hour ago rolls through here every September while tens of thousands cheer.

Above the racket, on the second floor of the temple on the square's west side, sits the reason to look up: Akash Bhairav, the sky god, a massive silver mask of a fierce, wide-eyed deity. Bhairav is Shiva in his terrifying form, and this one only shows his face properly during Indra Jatra, when the mask is displayed and the square fills with devotees drinking blessed rice beer from a sacred jar. The rest of the year he watches from behind the lattice, which is honestly more mysterious.

Practical advice for Indra Chowk: walk slowly, keep your bag in front, say no thank you to the third bangle seller with a smile, and buy the roasted corn from the street vendors if anyone is roasting it. You are now officially off the tourist track and into the working city. Next stop is two minutes north — a quieter courtyard with a whiter, calmer god.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A public market square. The Akash Bhairav shrine is viewed from outside; leave a small donation if you enter.
stops.openingHours: Market busiest roughly 09:00 to 19:00. The shrine opens for morning and evening worship.
stops.accessibility: Flat but crowded, with uneven paving, open drains at the edges and motorbikes. Not easy with wheels; go slowly.
stops.insiderTip: The bead and pote sellers on the north side will restring a broken necklace while you wait — a classic Indra Chowk errand that costs almost nothing.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north out of the square along the main lane for about two minutes, following signs for Jana Bahal. Turn into the temple courtyard with the white shrine and the stone water spouts. That is the White Machhendranath temple.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Maesi64, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: White Machhendranath, Jana Bahal
stops.narration:
Step through the archway and let the noise drop away. This is Jana Bahal, home of Seto Machhendranath — the White Machhendranath — and it is one of the valley's great multitasking gods.

To Buddhists he is Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. To Hindus he is a form of Vishnu. Nobody here sees a contradiction, and that easy double identity is the whole secret of Kathmandu Valley religion: the gods simply refuse to pick a team. His white-painted face looks out from the temple with famously kind eyes, and childless couples, students before exams, and anyone with a heavy week all come to ask favours.

Every spring, usually March or April, he gets the full treatment: the Jana Baha Dyah Jatra, when his image is installed in a towering wooden chariot and hauled through the old city for days, with babies held up to him for blessings and the route lined ten deep. If your timing is lucky, you will see the chariot timbers stored around the courtyard — they look like the scaffolding of some beautiful siege engine.

Before you leave, find the stone water spouts, the jahru, on the courtyard's edge. These carved conduits have delivered drinking water to this neighbourhood for centuries, fed by ancient royal canals, and the morning queue with brass water jars is one of the city's most photogenic rituals. This is also your last flat rest before the long western leg: from here we walk twenty minutes to the foot of Swayambhu hill. Fill your water bottle, use a restroom while there is a clean one, and set your legs to hill mode.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free courtyard. A small donation at the shrine is customary but not required.
stops.openingHours: Courtyard open in daylight hours. Morning worship is the liveliest time.
stops.accessibility: Level courtyard reached through an archway with a small step. The water-spout area can be wet and slippery.
stops.insiderTip: If the chariot timbers are stored here, ask a local which month the Jatra falls this year — the date follows the lunar calendar and shifts annually.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard and walk west along the Chhetrapati road for about twenty minutes, following signs for Swayambhu. Pass Chhetrapati Chowk, keep to the main road as it bends, and stop at the small tantric temple complex just before the hill rises. That is Bijeshwari.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rajesh Dhungana, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bijeshwari (Bajra Yogini) Temple
stops.narration:
You have walked the long western stretch and the hill is rising in front of you. Before the climb, stop here, because this small complex is the foothill's fierce guardian — and she deserves the respect of a visit before you march past.

Bijeshwari is a temple of Bajra Yogini, Vajrayogini, one of the great tantric goddesses of the valley, worshipped by Buddhists and Hindus with equal intensity. Tantric deities are not the gentle kind: they demand more from their devotees — early mornings, strict rituals, offerings with meaning — and in return they are considered faster, more direct, more powerful. The red-painted shrine, the butter lamps, the smell of incense and marigold: everything here runs a little hotter than the temples back in the square.

The complex sits in a walled compound with schools and rest houses around it, which gives it a village feel despite the city pressing in. Take five minutes on the bench by the courtyard. Watch the lamp-lighters, the students cutting through on their way home, the old men doing their evening rounds. This is neighbourhood religion, unperformed and daily, and it is the perfect palate cleanser.

Because what comes next is the opposite of quiet. The eastern stairway to Swayambhu starts just west of here: 365 stone steps up a forested hill, monkeys included. Drink some water. Tie your shoes properly. Greet the goddess on your way out — you are going to want her on your side for the climb.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter the compound. Small donations for butter lamps are customary.
stops.openingHours: Open daylight hours, liveliest in the morning and around sunset prayers.
stops.accessibility: Level compound with some steps at individual shrines. Fully step-free routes are limited.
stops.insiderTip: The small shops on the lane outside sell the best pre-climb provisions: roasted peanuts, water, and kukri-shaped souvenirs you absolutely do not need.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west to the base of the hill and find the great eastern stairway with the Buddha statues flanking its foot. Climb all 365 steps to the top — slowly, with rests at the landings. The stupa waits at the summit.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sangita21957, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Swayambhunath Stupa
stops.narration:
You made it. Three hundred and sixty-five steps, one for every day of the year, and now catch your breath, because the eyes are looking at you.

Those vast painted eyes on all four sides of the stupa's tower are the Buddha's eyes of wisdom and compassion, gazing out over the valley in every direction at once. Between them runs the curly symbol that is both the Nepali number one and a sign of unity — a reminder that there is exactly one truth, even if this hill has never been able to agree on which religion owns it. Legend says Swayambhu, the self-arisen one, began as a lotus blooming on a lake that filled the whole valley, until the bodhisattva Manjushri sliced the hills open to drain the waters and the lotus settled here as a flame. Geologists will tell you the valley really was a lake. The lotus part is between you and the hill.

This is one of the oldest religious sites in Nepal, some fifteen hundred years of continuous worship, and it belongs to everyone: Buddhists circle it clockwise spinning prayer wheels, Hindus honour the Harati temple beside it — a goddess of smallpox turned protector of children, which is quite the career change — and the monkeys, well, the monkeys own the place and merely tolerate the rest of us. Guard your snacks. I am serious. They run cons up here.

Walk the full circuit clockwise at least once, spinning the prayer wheels as you go. Then find a spot on the eastern edge and look back across the whole city you just walked — the palace towers, the temple roofs, the market smoke — with the Himalayas floating behind it all on a clear day. Gods, kings, hippies, markets and one long staircase. That was Kathmandu. And those eyes will be watching you all the way down.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay around Rs 200 at the ticket counter near the eastern stairway base. SAARC nationals pay less. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Hilltop open roughly sunrise to sunset, around 05:00 to 19:00. Come early or late for the best light and fewest monkeys with attitude.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: 365 steep stone steps with no lift, plus uneven paving and slopes at the summit. There is a longer vehicle road up the west side that avoids the steps but still involves slopes.
stops.insiderTip: For sunset, arrive at least an hour early and claim an eastern-edge spot — the sun drops behind the hills and the whole stupa turns gold while the city lights come on below.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Descend by the same eastern stairway, or take the western vehicle road down for a gentler slope. Taxis wait near both bases for the ride back to Thamel or Durbar Square.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Aritra360, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
